strengths: Addresses a timely and clearly motivated problem: the paper directly responds to Räisä et al. (2025)'s argument that all current fidelity/coverage metrics are flawed and none offer absolute interpretability.

The proposed modifications (capping individual sample contributions, clipping ball radii to the median NND, and normalization/calibration) are simple, well-explained, and grounded in concrete failure cases (Figure 2, Appendix D's analysis of RESFLOW's inflated Density of 2.47 traced to 4 real OOD images).

The paper includes a genuine theoretical contribution: Lemma 1 derives the expected value of the unnormalized Clipped Coverage under identical distributions via a Beta-Binomial argument, which is then used to calibrate the metric for linear degradation.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for a metrics paper: controlled sanity tests on CIFAR-10 and synthetic Gaussian data with multiple baselines, replication of the Räisä et al. (2025) benchmark with the original code, ablations quantifying each modification's effect (Appendix E), sensitivity to k, and evaluation across 4 real datasets and ~42 generated model sets.
Strong reproducibility: implementation details, verified equivalence with original metric implementations, computational requirements, and public data sources are all provided.
The medical imaging case study (Appendix F) illustrates a practical benefit of absolute interpretability that relative metrics cannot provide.
weaknesses: The claim of 'absolute interpretability' is stronger than the evidence. The linear-degradation calibration is validated primarily with 'bad' samples defined as OOD Gaussian noise images in a mixture. Real generative model deficiencies (mode dropping, subtle artifacts, distribution shift) need not degrade scores in the same calibrated way, so interpreting a score of x as 'equivalent to x good samples' is only meaningful for the specific bad-sample definition used.

Section 5.3 itself undercuts the absolute-interpretation claim: the authors observe that metric ranges correlate with training set size (CIFAR-10 max ≈ 0.4 vs ImageNet ≈ 1.0). If absolute values are dominated by reference set size rather than sample quality, the '40% good samples' interpretation for CIFAR-10/FFHQ may be an artifact of finite-sample kNN behavior rather than a true quality measure; this tension is acknowledged only implicitly.

The core method is largely a set of empirical patches (median radius clipping, leave-one-out real-data normalization, numerically computed calibration function g) rather than a principled estimator; the median choice is justified only heuristically, and the calibration for ClippedCoverage assumes bad samples always lie outside all real balls, which may not hold for realistic failure modes.

On the Räisä et al. (2025) benchmark (Appendix H), the proposed metrics still fail several tests (e.g., Discrete vs. Continuous Num., Hypercube varying sample size, Hypersphere Surface bounds), and the authors reclassify some of their failures as successes by contesting the benchmark's criteria (H.1/H.2); while the arguments are reasonable, this weakens the 'outperform existing methods' claim to 'fewer failures after criterion reinterpretation.'

Novelty is moderate: the metrics are incremental modifications of Density/Coverage (Naeem et al., 2020) rather than a new evaluation paradigm; the theoretical calibration component is the main novel technical element.

Some sensitivity experiments (e.g., matched OOD proportion tests in Figures 4c/5a) operate on very small score ranges (0.94–1.02), where modest std bands make pass/fail judgments in the summary tables harder to fully verify from the plots alone.

strengths: The paper directly addresses a timely and clearly stated open problem: the recent position paper by Räisä et al. (2025) argues that all existing fidelity/coverage metrics are flawed and none support absolute evaluation, and this work is a concrete, well-motivated attempt to fix that.

The metric construction is carefully done and goes beyond trivial clipping: radius clipping to the median NND (Eq. 5), per-sample contribution caps, leave-one-out normalization for Clipped Density, and a theoretically derived calibration function g (Lemma 1 with a correct Beta-Binomial argument in Appendix A) for Clipped Coverage.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for a metric paper: multiple sanity tests (mode dropping, matched OOD injection, Gaussian translation with planted outliers, progressive bad-sample mixing) on both toy Gaussian data and CIFAR-10/DINOv2 embeddings, comparison against roughly a dozen existing metrics, evaluation of 42 generated model outputs across four real datasets, a replication of the Räisä et al. benchmark, k-sensitivity analysis, and ablations tracing each modification from Density to Clipped Density (Tables 3–6).

Strong reproducibility practices: implementation comparisons against original author code (Table 1), exact-matching values, complexity analysis, and a detailed accounting of computational cost (~120 hours).
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited. The core contributions are (i) clipping per-sample scores at 1, (ii) clipping ball radii at the median, and (iii) recalibrating the score to enforce linearity. These are sensible but incremental engineering fixes on top of Density/Coverage (Naeem et al., 2020), and several prior works (Precision Recall Cover, symPrecision/Recall, P-precision/recall, TopP&R) already targeted similar failure modes. The theoretical component (Lemma 1) is a straightforward Beta-Binomial expectation computation.

The central 'absolute interpretability' claim is weaker than presented. The linear degradation property is achieved by construction against one particular operationalization of 'bad samples' (Gaussian-noise images planted in CIFAR-10, or samples placed outside all real balls in the theory). Whether a real model with score 0.4 genuinely 'has 40% good samples' for realistic quality degradations (subtle artifacts, mode dropping, distribution shift) is not demonstrated. Notably, Figure 4a shows most fidelity metrics already decrease roughly linearly, so the interpretability advantage over baselines is mainly established for coverage.

The paper's own real-dataset results undermine the absolute-interpretation claim: scores are reported to 'reflect the size of the training dataset' (CIFAR-10 ≈ 0.4, LSUN ≈ 0.7, ImageNet ≈ 1.0). If the maximum achievable score depends strongly on dataset size and the leave-one-out normalization constant ClippedDensity_real (which depends on N), then absolute values conflate model quality with reference-set properties — precisely the calibration problem the paper claims to solve.

Several design choices are heuristic and their justification is somewhat circular: the median radius clip (Eq. 5), capping Clipped Density at 1 after normalization, and the numerical calibration g (which is essentially a quantile remapping forced to yield 1−x). No analysis is given of sensitivity of the calibration to the distribution of 'bad' samples or to mismatch between the theoretical i.i.d. identical-distribution assumption (Lemma 1) and real settings.

The Appendix H benchmark comparison is partly self-serving: seven discrepancies with the original benchmark are attributed to hash-seed nondeterminism, and several of the authors' own failures are reclassified as 'harsh criteria' (H.1) or 'incorrect criterion' (H.2). This weakens the force of the claim that the proposed metrics pass the community benchmark; a neutral treatment or third-party verification would be more convincing.
No code release is stated, which for a paper whose main artifact is a pair of metrics is a notable reproducibility gap despite the otherwise detailed implementation description.

The Discussion acknowledges but does not resolve key open issues: the benchmark is admittedly non-exhaustive, embedding-model choice (DINOv2) is unexamined, and memorization is ignored — meaning a model could score well on Clipped Density while reproducing training data.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: a recent position paper (Räisä et al., 2025) argues that all existing fidelity/diversity metrics are flawed and none supports absolute evaluation, and this work directly tackles both concerns (outlier robustness and interpretable absolute scores).

The proposed metrics are simple, well-motivated modifications of Density/Coverage (clipping per-sample contributions, clipping ball radii to the median k-NN distance), and the intuition for each design choice is clearly explained with illustrative failure cases (e.g., Figure 2, the RESFLOW analysis in Appendix D).

There is genuine theoretical content: Lemma 1 derives the expected value of the unnormalized Clipped Coverage under identical distributions via a Beta-Binomial argument, and the calibration function g is constructed principledly from this derivation rather than by ad-hoc curve fitting.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for a metrics paper: multiple sanity-check scenarios on both real (CIFAR-10) and synthetic Gaussian data, comparison against nine baseline metrics with original code where available, evaluation on the Räisä et al. (2025) benchmark, and a large-scale study across four datasets and ~42 generative models.

Reproducibility and engineering rigor are strong: implementation equivalence with original codebases is verified numerically (Table 1), memory/time complexities are analyzed, computational costs are documented (~120 hours), and an efficient k-NN based implementation is provided.
Appendix analysis (e.g., Section D on the four outlier CIFAR-10 images inflating Density to 2.47) concretely demonstrates that the failure mode being fixed is real, not hypothetical.
The paper is honest about limitations (benchmark non-exhaustiveness, memorization not covered, embedding model choice as an open question).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a relatively incremental heuristic: capping per-sample contributions at 1 and clipping ball radii to the median. While effective, the design choices feel hand-tuned to pass the specific sanity tests used, raising concerns about overfitting the metric design to the evaluation suite (and the authors' own framing of which behaviors are 'desired').

The central 'absolute interpretability' claim is stronger than the evidence. The claim that a score of x means 'equivalent to x good samples and (1-x) bad samples' holds only when bad samples lie entirely outside all real balls and good samples behave like real data. In practice, model deficiencies exist on a spectrum, and the score conflates true badness with finite-sample effects: the paper itself notes the score range depends on training set size (CIFAR-10 max ≈ 0.4 vs ImageNet ≈ 1.0), which undermines reading 0.4 as '40% good samples' — a well-known sample-size-driven ceiling would produce the same number.

The Clipped Density calibration is empirical (normalization by the leave-one-out real-data score) and the Clipped Coverage calibration is numerical (sorting-based inversion of f_expected), so the guarantee of linearity/normalization is only exact under the idealized i.i.d.-identical-distribution setting and degrades in ways not theoretically characterized for realistic deviations.

The 'bad samples' used in tests are Gaussian noise images or distant Gaussian samples — trivially separable outliers. Sensitivity to subtler, more realistic quality deficiencies (blur, artifacts, partial distribution shift) is less demonstrated, and the aggressive radii clipping may over-correct (e.g., RESFLOW dropping from 2.47 to 0.00 fidelity), potentially discarding informative signal.

Results depend on hyperparameters (k) and the embedding model (DINOv2-ViT-L/14); the k-sensitivity study (Appendix K) shows scores shift substantially with k for all metrics, and no guidance is given on how absolute interpretation should account for this.
Evaluation is confined to the image domain; generalization of the interpretability claims to other modalities or embedding spaces is untested.

Some baseline behaviors in the summary tables (Figures 4e, 5c) involve judgment calls about what 'desired behavior' means (e.g., whether a fidelity metric 'should' respond to mode dropping), which occasionally reads as favorably defining the test criteria for the proposed metrics.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: the paper directly responds to the Rääsä et al. (2025) position paper's claim that all current fidelity/coverage metrics are flawed and none support absolute evaluation, and the proposed metrics are designed to fix precisely the identified shortcomings (outlier robustness, unbounded/uninterpretable scores).

The methodological changes (capping individual sample contributions, clipping ball radii to the median, and a theoretically derived calibration for Clipped Coverage via a Beta-Binomial analysis with a full proof of Lemma 1) are simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained.

Unusually comprehensive empirical validation: controlled sanity tests on CIFAR-10 and toy Gaussian data against ~15 baseline metrics, evaluation on four real generative model benchmarks (CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN Bedroom, FFHQ) with 40+ models, correlation with human error rates, evaluation on the Rääsä et al. benchmark using the authors' original code, sensitivity to k, sample-size stability (std ~ 1/√N), rare-mode and distortion tests, and additional modalities (time series, music, chest X-rays).

The absolute interpretability claim is supported empirically (linear degradation with proportion of bad samples on multiple datasets) and enables practically useful conclusions (e.g., no reference model needed; absolute assessment of a Chest X-ray GAN).
Strong reproducibility: code is released, exact-value comparisons with original implementations are provided (Table 1), datasets are publicly shared, and computational costs are documented in detail.
Analysis goes beyond aggregate scores (e.g., RESFLOW Density=2.47 traced to 4 outlier real images; sample-wise histograms for truncation/guidance effects), giving the paper good scientific depth.
weaknesses: The core contribution is conceptually incremental: two heuristic modifications (min-clipping of contributions, median radius clipping) applied to existing k-NN metrics, plus a numerical recalibration. Much of the value comes from careful evaluation rather than new insight.

The linearity/interpretability calibration rests on a strong and only partially examined assumption: that 'bad' samples always lie outside all real k-NN balls. Linear degradation is verified for clearly out-of-distribution noise; it is unclear the scores remain meaningfully interpretable for subtler failure modes (memorized samples, mild artifacts, slightly off-manifold samples), which are arguably the most common practical failures. The 'x% good samples' interpretation may therefore be overclaimed.

Median radius clipping for Clipped Density discards information about genuinely sparse/heavy-tailed real regions, potentially penalizing models that cover legitimate rare structure; the paper addresses rare modes only in an appendix and the trade-off of this design choice is not fully analyzed.

The theoretical calibration of Clipped Coverage is a numerical inversion of an expected-value curve parameterized by M and depends on k and sample sizes; the paper itself concedes no infinite-sample theoretical analysis, and the calibration's dependence on finite M (with floor/rounding effects) is not quantified for small reference sets.

On the Rääsä et al. benchmark the proposed metrics still fail several checks (e.g., Discrete vs. Continuous Num., Hypercube tests, One Disjoint Dim + Many Identical Dim., Hypersphere Surface), and the paper attributes some failures to overly strict criteria; this argumentation is somewhat self-serving and leaves the 'all flaws fixed' framing only partially established.

The human-evaluation correlation is essentially zero on FFHQ (r = -0.05), a limitation that is noted but not investigated; the metrics also inherit dependence on the embedding model (DINOv2), which remains an open confounder.

Several central claims (robustness, interpretability) are validated mostly on self-designed tests whose 'ideal' behavior is defined by the authors; broader independent validation on downstream-task utility of the absolute scores is missing.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: the recent position paper by Räisä et al. (2025) argues that all existing fidelity/coverage metrics are flawed and unsuitable for absolute evaluation, and this work directly and concretely responds to that call.

The proposed metrics are technically well-grounded: Clipped Density and Clipped Coverage are derived from a clear set of desiderata, and the calibration of Clipped Coverage is supported by an actual theoretical analysis (Lemma 1 with a Beta-Binomial argument), not purely empirical curve fitting.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough: controlled metric sanity tests (bad-sample introduction, mode dropping, matched OOD samples, synthetic distribution translation), evaluation of 40+ generative models across four image datasets, comparison against the Räisä et al. benchmark, robustness to k and sample size, additional modalities (time series, music), rare-mode failure scenarios, and human-evaluation correlation analysis.
Strong reproducibility: implementation details, computational costs, exact settings, comparison tables against original metric implementations, and a stated public code release.

Many prior metrics' failure modes are clearly demonstrated (e.g., Density scores of 2.47 driven by four real OOD samples, sensitivity of α-Precision/P-precision, non-symmetric behavior of Recall under outliers), which is valuable analysis independent of the proposed metrics.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is relatively incremental: the metrics are Density/Coverage with (i) per-sample contribution clipping and (ii) radius clipping to the median. These are sensible but heuristic fixes; the median choice for radii clipping is somewhat ad hoc and its justification is more intuitive than principled.

The headline property of 'linear score degradation' is largely engineered by construction: Clipped Coverage is calibrated by inverting its own expected-value curve, so the linearity of the calibrated metric on tests built from the same mixture assumption is somewhat circular; absolute interpretability claims rest on the questionable premise that 'bad' samples always lie outside any real ball and are otherwise ignored by the metric.

The absolute-score interpretation is validated mostly on synthetic mixtures (real samples + noise). How well the interpretation transfers to genuinely bad synthetic samples (subtly distorted, mode-collapsed, or memorized outputs) is less clear, and the empirical observation that maximum scores track training-set size (CIFAR-10 ≈ 0.4, ImageNet ≈ 1.0) suggests the calibration may be sensitive to the reference dataset rather than an intrinsic quality measure.
The claim that a score of x is 'equivalent to a proportion x of good samples' is a relatively coarse interpretability guarantee and may be oversold in the abstract and introduction.

Some empirical results weaken the narrative: the FFHQ human-correlation result is null (r = -0.05 / 0.24, p > 0.5), and several benchmark failures in Appendix H are dismissed by reinterpreting the benchmark's criteria, which a skeptical reader may view as post-hoc rationalization.

No theoretical analysis of the metrics in the infinite-sample limit is provided (acknowledged by the authors), so the behavior of the calibrated scores as N and M grow, and their interaction with the radius-clipping estimator, remains uncharacterized.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: Räisä et al. (2025) argued that all existing fidelity/coverage metrics are flawed and none supports absolute interpretation; this paper directly targets both shortcomings with concrete new metrics.

The proposed modifications (capping individual sample contributions, clipping ball radii to the median k-NN distance for fidelity, fixed-mass balls for coverage) are well-motivated by clear failure cases (e.g., Figure 2, the RESFLOW Density=2.47 analysis in Section D).

Includes a genuine theoretical contribution: a closed-form derivation of the expected ClippedCoverage behavior (Lemma 1) with a correct and complete proof using Beta-Binomial order statistics, enabling principled calibration to linear degradation rather than purely empirical curve-fitting.

Very comprehensive evaluation: controlled sanity tests on CIFAR-10 and toy data across many scenarios (bad-sample introduction, mode dropping, matched OOD proportions, Gaussian translation), comparison against ~10 baseline metrics, evaluation on 42 generated datasets across four benchmarks, correlation with human judgments, the Räisä et al. benchmark, k-sensitivity, sample-size stability (1/√N), truncation/guidance trade-off, and other modalities (time series, music).

Strong reproducibility: code release, detailed implementation comparison with original metric implementations, computational cost accounting, and public data sources; reimplementations verified to match original values exactly.
Insightful discussion of edge cases (Section K) explaining why scores exceed 1 for guided/truncated models and justifying the clipping choice; honest limitations section.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is relatively incremental: clipping individual contributions and ball radii are simple, heuristic modifications of existing Density/Coverage metrics rather than a fundamentally new evaluation framework.

The absolute interpretability claim ('score x = equivalent to proportion x of good samples') depends on a constructed notion of 'bad' samples (noise images/embeddings in the calibration); the equivalence is only calibrated for this particular type of degradation, and its generality to qualitatively different failure modes (e.g., subtle distortions, invented modes) is not fully established.

Several benchmark tests from Räisä et al. (2025) are still failed, and the paper dismisses some of these as 'harsh criteria' or 'incorrect criteria' (Section H.1/H.2); while the arguments are reasonable, reinterpreting failures after the fact weakens the benchmark evidence.

The absolute scores are strongly sample-size and reference-set dependent: max scores correlate with training set size (0.4 for CIFAR-10 vs 1.0 for ImageNet), so the claimed absolute interpretation requires large, high-quality reference sets that many practitioners will not have; no theoretical infinite-sample analysis is provided (acknowledged by the authors).
Results depend on the DINOv2 embedding choice, and the human-evaluation correlation is absent on FFHQ; embedding-model sensitivity is acknowledged but not resolved.

Much of the evidence (benchmark comparison, calibration stability, robustness analyses) is relegated to the appendix; the main text summary tables (Figures 4e, 5c) compress a lot of nuance into binary pass/fail judgments that favor the proposed metrics.
